421.title: The night song
421.hook: Sohila means song of praise; its five hymns close the day and close a life
421.carry: a song of joy, for the last night
421.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep, often in bed; it is recited when the Guru Granth Sahib is put to rest in many gurdwaras and at the cremation of a Sikh, followed by Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nitnem, and your line, both ends held. Did you keep a bookend at each end of the day? Today a new stretch begins: the last prayer before sleep. Day four hundred twenty-one.

A lot of homes have a bedtime song. A grandmother humming in the dark, a father singing the same three lines every night, badly, because the baby likes them. The words matter less than the fact that they're the last thing heard before sleep. The day has a lot of voices in it. The night song is the one that gets the final word. Sikhs have one too, and it's sung not only at the end of a day. Today: the night song.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER HUMMING IN THE DARK.` → `THE LAST THING HEARD BEFORE SLEEP.` → `THE NIGHT SONG GETS THE FINAL WORD.`

segments.voice: It's called Kirtan Sohila, or simply Sohila. Sohila is usually explained as a song of praise, and in old Punjabi it was also a word for joyful songs, the kind sung at weddings. It's short: five shabads, on pages twelve and thirteen of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after Rehras in the book. The first three are by Guru Nanak, the fourth by Guru Ram Das, the fifth by Guru Arjan. The Sikh code of conduct places it at night, before going to sleep. Some say it in bed with the light off, or play it softly as children fall asleep. And it closes more than a day. In gurdwaras, Kirtan Sohila is recited when the Guru Granth Sahib is put to rest at night. And when a Sikh dies, Kirtan Sohila is recited at the cremation, followed by Ardas. The same five hymns at bedtime and at a funeral. That's not gloomy. Some Sikh teachers describe sleep and death as both a kind of letting go, a handing of yourself back to the One, and the night song meets them with the same calm. The first hymn even speaks of a day fixed in advance, the way a wedding date is written, and the friends gathering to bless the one setting out. A song of joy for the night, and for the last night. Over the next two weeks we'll take the five hymns one at a time, each by its sound and then its meaning. Tonight, just know what it is. The night song.
screen: `SOHILA: A SONG OF PRAISE, OF JOY.` · `FIVE SHABADS, THREE GURUS, ANG 12–13.` · `BEFORE SLEEP, AND AT THE CREMATION.` · `SLEEP AND DEATH: HANDED BACK IN CALM.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it before bed. Tonight, if you can find Kirtan Sohila on your phone, in a gutka, or as a recording, read or listen to it once, lying down, lights low. It takes only a few minutes. If you'd rather not tonight, picture yourself in bed, the day finished, and let one line you've learned on this path be the last thing you hear: anand bhaiaa, or hamree karo haath dai rachhaa. For now, rest. Let your body grow heavy, as if night has already come. The bell holds the time.
Sohila. Kirtan Sohila, the Sikh night song: five shabads of praise said before sleep, and recited at the end of a life.
Your line: a song of joy, for the last night. Tonight, let the last thing you hear before sleep be chosen: Sohila, or one line from this path, instead of the phone. Day four hundred twenty-one.

422.title: Hymn 1, sound: jai ghar keerat
422.hook: jai ghar keerat aakheeai kartey kaa hoe beechaaro (Gauri Deepaki M1, ang 12)
422.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep, beginning with this hymn of Guru Nanak; in gurdwaras it is sung when the Guru Granth Sahib is closed and laid to rest for the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sohila, a song of joy, for the last night: five hymns that close the day. Did you read or hear it before bed? Today we open the first of the five, and we start with its sound. Day four hundred twenty-two.
screen: `SOHILA — A SONG OF JOY, FOR THE LAST NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Every house has a sound. The kettle in the morning. A television murmuring in the next room. Somebody's music through a closed door, the same three songs on repeat. If a stranger stood in your hallway for an hour with their eyes shut, they would know a lot about who lives there. The first hymn of Sohila begins in a house too. It doesn't describe a temple, or a mountain, or a holy city. It describes a house, any house, by what is heard inside it. Today: the opening line, sound first.
screen: `EVERY HOUSE HAS A SOUND.` → `WHAT WOULD A STRANGER HEAR?` → `HYMN 1 BEGINS IN A HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, slowly: jai ghar keerat aakheeai, kartey kaa hoe beechaaro. It's by Guru Nanak, in Raag Gauri Deepaki, on Ang 12 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Take it word by word. Jai ghar: in the house where. Keerat: praise. Aakheeai: is spoken. Kartey kaa: of the Creator. Hoe beechaaro: and there is reflection, real thought about the One. So: in the house where the Creator's praise is spoken and reflected on. The next line finishes the thought: in that house, sing Sohila, and remember the One who made you. Notice the pairing. Not only praise, but praise and reflection together. Words that are said, and words that are thought about. Then comes the refrain, the line the whole hymn keeps returning to. In paraphrase: sing the song of praise of my Fearless One; I would give myself for that song, which brings lasting peace. Fearless is nirbhau, the same word you met in the Mool Mantar at the very start of the path. One more layer in the first line. Ghar can mean a building, but in Gurbani it also points inward: the heart, the body, a gathering of people. So jai ghar is a house with a door and a kettle, and it is also you. Some readers hear it both ways. The house where praise is sung might be a gurdwara, a kitchen, or the inside of one tired person at eleven at night. The Guru doesn't say which house. He says what kind.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first line aloud. Jai ghar keerat aakheeai, kartey kaa hoe beechaaro. Say it once just for the sound, letting the syllables come slowly. Then say it again and listen to the room you're in while you say it. What else does this house sound like right now? A fridge, traffic, a dog? Let the line sit among those sounds. Then be quiet and breathe, and let the room go on sounding. If you pray, you can whisper the line once more at the end. The bell holds the time.
Keerat, praise: the first of Sohila's five, by Guru Nanak: in the house where the Creator's praise is spoken and reflected on, in that house, sing.

Your line: jai ghar keerat. In the house where praise is sung. Tonight, before bed, notice what your home sounds like in its last hour, and let one good word be part of it. Day four hundred twenty-two.

423.title: Oil at the threshold
423.hook: in the house where praise is sung, friends pour oil at the door for the bride, whose day has come (Gauri Deepaki M1, ang 12)
423.howItsDone: Sikhs recite these verses every night as the close of Kirtan Sohila's first hymn, and Kirtan Sohila is also recited at a Sikh cremation; some Punjabi families still keep the custom of pouring oil at the threshold when a bride or groom arrives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was jai ghar keerat: in the house where praise is sung. What did your home sound like in its last hour? Today, the same hymn, its last verses. Day four hundred twenty-three.
screen: `JAI GHAR KEERAT — IN THE HOUSE OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: A Punjabi wedding doesn't start on the wedding day. It starts weeks before, with a date. Someone fixes the auspicious day, it gets written down, and letters go out. Then the house fills up: cousins, aunties, songs every evening, turmeric, laughter, too much food. And at the doorway there is a small custom some families still keep. When the bride or the groom arrives at the threshold, a woman of the house pours a little oil on either side of the door, as a welcome and a blessing. Guru Nanak puts that whole scene at the end of the night song's first hymn.
screen: `THE DATE IS FIXED AND WRITTEN.` → `SONGS EVERY EVENING.` → `OIL POURED AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The last verses of Sohila's first hymn sound like a wedding invitation. In paraphrase: the year and the moment have been written; come, friends, together, pour the oil. Give me your blessings, friends, so that I may meet my Lord. The word for that fixed date is saahaa, the wedding day set in advance. In Gurbani the soul is often pictured as a bride, and God as the beloved she longs to meet. So who is the bride here? The soul. And what is the wedding? The meeting with the One. Then the hymn turns, gently. In paraphrase again: into every house this message is sent; these calls come every day. Remember the One who sends the call, says Nanak; those days are drawing near. Commentators read the wedding here as death, the soul's day to go and meet the Beloved. Read that way, the verse belongs in a night song, and every night becomes a small rehearsal of letting go. But the mood is not dread. It's a wedding. The friends aren't weeping at the door; they're pouring oil and giving blessings. Notice, too, that the summons isn't sent to one unlucky house. It goes to every house, every day. Nobody is singled out. Nobody is skipped. The hymn doesn't ask you to fear the letter. It asks you to be the kind of house where praise is sung when it arrives, and to have friends at the door when it's your turn.
screen: `THE DATE IS WRITTEN: SAAHAA.` · `THE SOUL AS THE BRIDE.` · `A CALL TO EVERY HOUSE, EVERY DAY.` · `FRIENDS AT THE DOOR WITH BLESSINGS.` · then, large: `THE BRIDE IS CALLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless someone's doorway. Picture a door you know well: a parent's front door, a friend's apartment, a neighbor's gate, your own. See it clearly, the handle, the step, the light. Now imagine standing there as one of the friends in the hymn, wishing whoever lives inside well. Not a speech. Just: may this house be well. Hold that wish while you breathe. Then move to one more door if you like. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly for the people behind it. The bell holds the time.
Saahaa, the fixed wedding date: the wedding welcome Guru Nanak places at the end of Sohila's first hymn, where friends bless the bride, the soul, whose day has been written.

Your line: the bride is called. Today, when you walk through a door, your own or anyone's, let it remind you that the call comes to every house, and wish the house well. Day four hundred twenty-three.

424.title: Hymn 2, sound: chhia ghar
424.hook: chhia ghar chhia gur chhia updes (Asa M1, ang 12)
424.howItsDone: This is the second of the five hymns Sikhs recite each night in Kirtan Sohila; in gurdwaras it is recited when the Guru Granth Sahib is put to rest for the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saahaa, the fixed wedding date, and your line: the bride is called. Did a doorway remind you to wish a house well? Today, Sohila's second hymn, sound first. Day four hundred twenty-four.

Some lines are built like a drumbeat. You hear the pattern before you understand a single word. Chhia ghar. Chhia gur. Chhia updes. Three beats, and the same little word starts each one. Even if you've never heard a word of Punjabi, you can tell something is being counted. That's the second hymn of Sohila, also by Guru Nanak, this time in Raag Asa, still on Ang 12. Yesterday's hymn was gentle, full of a wedding. This one opens short and sharp, like someone tapping a table three times to get the room's attention. Today: what's being counted.
screen: `A LINE BUILT LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` → `CHHIA, CHHIA, CHHIA.` → `SOMETHING IS BEING COUNTED.`

segments.voice: The first line: chhia ghar chhia gur chhia updes. Chhia means six. Ghar you met two days ago: a house. Here it means a house of thought, a school. Gur is a teacher. Updes is a teaching, instruction. So: six schools, six teachers, six teachings. Then the second line answers the drumbeat: gur gur eko ves anek. The Guru of those gurus is One; the forms are many. Eko means one, like the Ik of Ik Onkar. Ves means a form, a dress, a guise. Anek means many. So in two lines Guru Nanak counts six, and then lands on one. Then comes the refrain, the line this hymn keeps returning to. In paraphrase: O Baba, the house in which the Creator's praise is sung, hold on to that house; in it lies your greatness. Hear the echo? Yesterday's hymn began with the house where praise is sung. Today's refrain comes back to the same house. In Sohila the hymns talk to each other, and the word ghar runs through both like a thread. Tomorrow we'll ask who the six schools were and what it means that one Guru wears many forms. Today, just keep the shape: six, six, six, and then one. A count that ends in unity.
screen: `CHHIA: SIX. GHAR: A SCHOOL.` · `SIX TEACHERS, SIX TEACHINGS.` · `GUR GUR EKO: ONE GURU OF GURUS.` · `THE HOUSE OF PRAISE, AGAIN.` · then, large: `CHHIA GHAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first line aloud. Chhia ghar, chhia gur, chhia updes. Say it slowly once, giving each beat its own space. Then say it again and tap a finger with each chhia: one, two, three. Then say the answer line: gur gur eko ves anek. Let your hand rest flat on that one. Now sit quietly, and feel the difference between counting and resting. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once as you breathe out. The bell holds the time.
Updes, a teaching: Sohila's second hymn, by Guru Nanak in Raag Asa, six schools, six teachers, six teachings, and one Guru of gurus in many forms.

Your line: chhia ghar. Six houses. Today, when you notice how many voices are telling you what to think, count them if you like, and then remember the line that comes after the count. Day four hundred twenty-four.

425.title: Six schools, one Guru
425.hook: six schools, six teachers, six teachings, but one Guru of gurus in many forms (Asa M1, ang 12)
425.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn every night in Kirtan Sohila, and its line about one Guru in many forms is often quoted in Sikh teaching on respect for other paths.

segments.voice: Yesterday, updes, a teaching, and your line: chhia ghar. Six, six, six, and then one. Did you count the voices around you? Today, who the six were. Day four hundred twenty-five.

Picture Guru Nanak's world as a crowded marketplace of ideas. Pandits arguing logic. Yogis with ash-smeared bodies and split ears. Philosophers debating whether the world is real or a kind of dream. Ritual experts measuring every syllable of an ancient chant. Each group had its own house, its own teacher, its own instruction. It's a question you may know from a bookstore's religion aisle: so many voices, which one do I listen to? Sohila's second hymn walks into that marketplace. And it doesn't pick a stall.
screen: `A MARKETPLACE OF IDEAS.` → `EACH HOUSE, ITS OWN TEACHER.` → `THE HYMN DOESN'T PICK A STALL.`

segments.voice: Chhia ghar, six schools. Many Sikh commentators read these as the six classical schools of Indian philosophy, the darshanas: Nyaya, which studies logic; Vaisheshika, which studies the parts the world is made of; Samkhya and Yoga; Mimamsa, the study of ritual; and Vedanta. Other commentators read the six as six orders of ascetics and their ways of life. Either way, the hymn is naming the great schools and orders of the Indian world around it. Now the move. It doesn't say five of the six are wrong. It says: gur gur eko, ves anek. The Guru of all these gurus is One, wearing many forms. Then a picture to show it, which we'll open tomorrow: many seasons, one sun. So the six teachers aren't rivals for the one prize. They're different garments on the same wearer. That's a striking thing to say in a marketplace where each stall is shouting. It fits the way Sikhs remember Guru Nanak. The janamsakhis, the old stories of his life, show him sitting with yogis, pandits and Sufis, asking questions, answering in song. The point the hymn makes is not that every teaching is identical. It's that the One is behind them all, and that the true teacher is the One. Which brings back the refrain: hold on to the house where the Creator's praise is sung. Whatever door you came in by, that's the house the hymn keeps pointing to.
screen: `SIX SCHOOLS: THE DARSHANAS.` · `NOT FIVE WRONG AND ONE RIGHT.` · `DIFFERENT GARMENTS, ONE WEARER.` · `THE HOUSE WHERE PRAISE IS SUNG.` · then, large: `ONE GURU, MANY FORMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect one path unlike yours. Think of a way of living or praying that isn't yours. Maybe a neighbor's faith, a friend's meditation, a grandparent's rituals. Picture a real person who walks it, and something good you've seen in them: patience, generosity, steadiness. Hold that picture for a few breaths without arguing with it. Then let the hymn's line sit beside it: one Guru, many forms. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly. The bell holds the time.
Six schools. The six houses of thought named in Sohila's second hymn, each with its teacher and teaching, and behind them, the hymn says, one Guru in many forms.
Your line: one guru, many forms. Today, when someone explains life in a way you wouldn't, listen for one thing in it that rings true before you answer. Day four hundred twenty-five.

426.title: Many seasons, one sun
426.hook: seconds, hours, days and seasons are many, but the sun is one (Asa M1, ang 12)
426.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this verse each night as the close of Kirtan Sohila's second hymn, and its image of one sun and many seasons is a common illustration in Sikh teaching about the one Creator and many forms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the six schools, and your line: one guru, many forms. Did you hear something true in a view unlike yours? Today, the picture Guru Nanak uses to show it. Day four hundred twenty-six.

Open the calendar on your phone. Seconds tick into minutes, minutes into hours. There's a Monday and a Thursday, a March and a November, a summer that feels nothing like winter. It all looks like a crowd of different things. Some days feel like they belong to a completely different life than others. And yet every one of those units is measured by the same thing: the sun coming up, the sun going down, the earth tilting toward it and away. Sohila's second hymn ends with that same observation, made long before anyone had a phone.
screen: `SECONDS, MONDAYS, NOVEMBERS.` → `A CROWD OF DIFFERENT TIMES.` → `ALL MEASURED BY ONE SUN.`

segments.voice: The closing verse of the hymn is a list of time, from tiny to huge. Visue and chasiaa: the smallest units of the old Indian clock, flickers of a moment. Gharhiaa: the ghari, a slice of the old Indian day. Pahraa: the pahar, one of the watches the day and night were divided into. Thitee: the lunar days. Vaaree: the weekdays. Maahu: the months. Every one of them, the verse says, comes into being. Then the turn: sooraj eko rut anek. The sun is one; the seasons are many. And the last line: Nanak, so many are the Creator's forms. That's the picture behind yesterday's six schools. Nobody calls summer false because winter is real, or makes Thursday compete with Saturday. They're all the one sun, seen at different angles. In the same way, the hymn says, the many forms are the play of one Creator. Notice what the image does for an ordinary week. A day of bad news and a day of laughing until it hurts are, in the hymn's picture, lit by the same sun; neither falls outside the One. Some Sikh teachers link this to hukam, the Creator's order running through everything, which came up early in the path. The seasons don't argue about who's in charge. They turn. Winter doesn't apologize for not being summer. It takes its turn under the same light, and then it hands the light on.
screen: `A LIST OF TIME, TINY TO HUGE.` · `SOORAJ EKO: THE SUN IS ONE.` · `NANAK: SO MANY FORMS.` · `EVERY DAY IS THE SAME LIGHT.` · then, large: `ONE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the sun's light today. Not at the sun itself, that's hard on your eyes. Look at what it touches. Light on a wall, on a leaf, on the floor through a window, on the back of your own hand. If it's night where you are, look at a lamp and remember tomorrow morning. Notice that the light on the wall and the light on your hand come from one place. Rest there for a few breaths. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly. The bell holds the time.
Many seasons. The close of Sohila's second hymn: seconds, hours, days, months and seasons are many, but the sun is one, and so many are the Creator's forms.
Your line: one sun. Today, when one hour feels nothing like the hour before it, look for the light, and remember it's the same sun on both. Day four hundred twenty-six.

the seasons are endless and have no source.
only the present moment matters.
fork.reveal: sooraj eko rut anek: one sun, many seasons, and so many are the Creator's forms.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sooraj, the sun; in the hymn, the one source of every season.

trapdoor: what you thought: many seasons, one sun is a nature line about the weather.
what it means: all the units of time come from one sun, as all forms come from one Creator.
what a scholar hears: the verse runs the traditional Indian time units (visua, chasa, ghari, pahar, thit, vaar, maah, rut) up to 'sooraj eko rut anek'.

sources.ref: Asa M1, Ang 12–13 (Kirtan Sohila, hymn 2, closing verse)

427.title: Hymn 3, sound: gagan mai thaal
427.hook: gagan mai thaal rav chand deepak bane (Dhanasri M1, ang 13)
427.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly as the third of Kirtan Sohila's five, and in many gurdwaras it is also sung on its own in the evening, often called the Aarti.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was one sun: many seasons, one light. And this is a week's end. This week you met Sohila's first two hymns: the house of praise, the bride called, six schools, one sun. Today, hymn three. Day four hundred twenty-seven.
screen: `ONE SUN.` · `A WEEK: THE HOUSE, THE BRIDE, THE SIX, THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Lie on your back outside on a clear night and the sky stops being a ceiling. It becomes a bowl, curved over you from edge to edge. Sohila's third hymn starts from that angle. It's by Guru Nanak, set in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 13, and its very first word is gagan, the sky. Its first line is a picture you could almost hold in two hands. Today: just the sound of that first line.
screen: `THE SKY AS A BOWL.` → `IT OPENS ON ONE WORD: SKY.` → `GURU NANAK LOOKS UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening: gagan mai thaal, rav chand deepak bane. Word by word. Gagan: the sky, the whole vault of the heavens. Mai: in, or made of. Thaal: a platter, the round metal tray you'd carry food or offerings on. Rav: the sun. You met the sun yesterday as sooraj; rav is another old name for it. Chand: the moon. Deepak: lamps, the little flames set on a tray. Bane: have become. So: the sky is the platter, and the sun and moon have become its lamps. The line keeps going, and we'll open the rest tomorrow, but even this much is a whole picture. Somebody is holding a tray of light. The tray is the sky. The lamps are the two great lights we live by. Notice how the week has built to this. This week's first hymn began in a house. The second hymn walked through the six schools and ended at the sun. Now the third hymn takes the sun and moon and sets them on a platter, like an offering. Sohila keeps widening the frame: a doorway, a marketplace, the calendar, and now the whole sky. Notice the words themselves too. Gagan, thaal, rav, chand, deepak: short, plain words, and each one an object you could point to.
screen: `GAGAN: THE SKY.` · `THAAL: A PLATTER OF LIGHT.` · `RAV AND CHAND: SUN AND MOON.` · `DEEPAK: THE LAMPS.` · then, large: `GAGAN MAI THAAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first line aloud. Gagan mai thaal, rav chand deepak bane. Say it once slowly, one word at a time: gagan, mai, thaal, rav, chand, deepak, bane. Then say it again, and as you do, picture a round tray held up in both hands, with two flames on it. Now let the tray grow until it's the size of the sky. Rest in that picture and just breathe. If you pray, you can say the line once more at the end. The bell holds the time.
Gagan, the sky: Sohila's third hymn, by Guru Nanak in Raag Dhanasri, the sky is the platter, and the sun and moon have become its lamps.
Your line: gagan mai thaal. The sky is the platter. Tonight, say the line once under your breath before you sleep. Day four hundred twenty-seven.

screen: `DAY 427 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.`

fork.setup: Guru Nanak looks up at the sky. what does the first line make of it?
options: a roof that hides God.
a platter, with the sun and moon as its lamps.
an empty space with nothing in it.
fork.reveal: gagan mai thaal, rav chand deepak bane: the sky is a tray of offering, and sun and moon are its lamps.

original.note: Gurmukhi: gagan, the sky; the first word of Sohila's third hymn.

trapdoor: what you thought: gagan mai thaal is a line of nature poetry.
what it means: the sky is held up like a tray of offering, with the sun and moon as its lamps.
what a scholar hears: the hymn is in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 13; thaal and deepak are the platter and lamps used in a temple aarti.
